title: August and the Well
premise: Felix Reyes, a meticulous new teacher at Hollow Creek Elementary, notices students vanishing from attendance records while everyone else remembers them as never having existed. His grandmother's old photographs begin showing an extra wooden chair, and the chair moves closer in each print. Digging into the town's sealed 1974 case files, Felix learns the school's founding principal drowned six children in the well beneath the gymnasium to protect his reputation, and their unresolved spirits have been reclaiming one living child per generation as payment. To end it, Felix must descend the well and return the principal's hidden confession ledger to the descendants of the victims—but the well demands a keeper, and Felix must choose between escaping alone or binding himself as the town's new witness so the children can finally rest.
about_author: Astrid Hartwell is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in small-town districts where records had a way of going missing. She writes horror about institutions, archives, and the debts communities refuse to acknowledge.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Felix Reyes arrives at Hollow Creek Elementary and begins his ritual of photographing every document he touches. A student named Marisol appears on his roster but no other teacher recalls her. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: quiet unease masked by professional competence.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting his late grandmother's belongings, Felix finds family photos now containing an empty wooden chair that wasn't there before; in successive prints it sits nearer. Marisol stops coming to class, and her desk is gone by morning. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: dread crystallizing into certainty.

chapters.title: Sealed in 1974
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Felix finds the 1974 disappearance file—six children, one night, all records expunged by court order signed by Principal Aldous Wren. The archivist warns him some documents read people back. POV: Felix with brief archive-clerk interlude. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery curdling into being watched.

chapters.title: What the Gym Sits On
chapters.summary: The janitor, Ruth, shows Felix the bricked-over well shaft beneath the gymnasium floor and admits the school pays her to pour salt down it monthly. That night the chair appears in a photo taken inside Felix's own classroom. POV: alternating Felix and Ruth. Emotional beat: complicity and fear.

chapters.title: Marisol's Voice
chapters.summary: Marisol contacts Felix through recorded classroom audio, speaking in overlapping voices of the six lost children, asking him to bring back what was taken. He realizes the chair is a summons—and an invitation list. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: grief and terrible responsibility.

chapters.title: The Wren Estate
chapters.summary: Felix tracks down Wren's surviving daughter, Eleanor, who has spent her life denying her father's crimes. Under pressure—and under the chair's growing presence in her own photographs—she reveals where the confession ledger is hidden. POV: Eleanor primarily. Emotional beat: denial breaking into shame.

chapters.title: Ledger
chapters.summary: Felix recovers the ledger from the sealed crawlspace of the old Wren house; reading it aloud nearly pulls him through, the words rearranging the room into 1974. The school board, corrupted by legacy money, tries to have him fired and the ledger destroyed. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: isolation, resolve hardening.

chapters.title: One Child Per Generation
chapters.summary: Ruth confesses the town's bargain: each generation offers a child to keep the well quiet, and this year's offering date is Friday. The townspeople, complicit for fifty years, turn on Felix when he refuses to let Marisol be taken. POV: Ruth and Felix. Emotional beat: moral horror of collective guilt.

chapters.title: The Well Keeps What It Is Owed
chapters.summary: Climax. Felix descends the well during the offering, ledger in hand, and reads the confession aloud in the dark while the drowned children surround him and Wren's preserved will-to-power manifests as a pressure trying to make him kneel. He returns what was taken—the truth, spoken where it was buried. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into testimony.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Resolution. The children pass on; Marisol is remembered back into existence, her records restored. The well stands open but quiet, needing a witness rather than a victim—and Felix stays, the town's keeper of records, photographing everything so it can never again be unwritten. Final image: a new photo with no extra chair. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: sorrowful peace, chosen vigilance.
